title: I/O software and disk scheduling
subtitle: Devices are slow and strange. The OS hides that with layers — and orders disk requests to keep the head from wandering.

sections.title: The I/O software stack
sections.body: Device-independent code (naming, buffering, protection) sits above a driver that knows one device's registers, which talks to the controller and raises an interrupt when a transfer ends. Three ways to move data: programmed I/O (the CPU polls), interrupt-driven (the CPU does other work and is interrupted), and DMA (a controller copies the whole block to memory and interrupts once).

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of DMA over interrupt-driven I/O for a large block?

choices.text: One interrupt for the whole block instead of one per byte/word.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The disk is as slow as before; the CPU just does not babysit it.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The controller moves the data itself, so the CPU is interrupted once at the end.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: A driver still sets up the transfer.

sections.title: How a disk spends its time
sections.body: A magnetic disk access is seek time (move the arm to the cylinder) + rotational latency (wait for the sector to come under the head) + transfer time. Seek dominates, so schedulers reorder requests to shorten head travel. SSDs have no arm, so these algorithms matter for spinning disks.

worked.why: A 7200 rpm disk turns once every 60/7200 s = 8.33 ms. On average the wanted sector is half a turn away.

questions.prompt: Which component of disk access do scheduling algorithms try to reduce?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Fixed by the recording density and spin speed.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Partly reducible by other tricks, but arm scheduling targets seeks.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Arm movement is the largest term, and it depends on the order requests are served.

sections.title: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, LOOK
sections.body: Head at 53, requests 98 183 37 122 14 124 65 67 on a 200-cylinder disk. FCFS serves in arrival order: 640 cylinders. SSTF always picks the nearest request: 236, but can starve far requests. SCAN (elevator) sweeps to one end then reverses; LOOK reverses at the last request: going up first costs 299. The circular versions (C-SCAN, C-LOOK) jump back and serve in one direction only — C-LOOK 322 — for more uniform waiting.

questions.prompt: Which policy can starve a request?

choices.text: SSTF — a steady stream of nearby requests keeps the far one waiting.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Shortest seek greedily serves neighbours; SCAN-style sweeps bound the wait to one pass.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: It visits every cylinder on each sweep, so nothing waits more than about two sweeps.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: FCFS is fair in order, merely slow.

problems.prompt: Head at 53, queue 98 183 37 122 14 124 65 67. Total head movement for SSTF and for FCFS?

sections.title: RAID in one page
sections.body: RAID 0 stripes data across disks (speed, no safety). RAID 1 mirrors (survives one failure, half the capacity). RAID 5 stripes with distributed parity: the parity block is the XOR of the data blocks, so any one lost block is recoverable; usable capacity is (n−1)/n.

worked.why: Three data blocks 1011, 0110, 1100. Parity is the bitwise XOR.
If the second disk dies, XOR the others with the parity: 1011 ⊕ 1100 ⊕ 0001 = 0110 — recovered.

questions.prompt: Usable capacity of RAID 5 with five 1 TB disks?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: One disk’s worth of space holds parity: (5−1)/5 × 5 TB.

sections.title: Stable storage
sections.body: A single disk write can be interrupted by a crash, leaving a half-written block. Stable storage makes a write all-or-nothing by keeping two copies: write copy A and verify it, then write copy B and verify it. After a crash, recovery compares the pair — if they differ and one has a bad checksum, copy the good one over it; if both are good but different, copy A to B. At most one copy is ever damaged, so a good value always survives.

questions.prompt: Why are two copies written one after the other rather than together?

choices.text: So a crash can damage at most one of them.
Disks cannot write two blocks at once.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It is slower; safety is the point.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Sequential writes guarantee that one copy is always intact and verified.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Independent disks can; the ordering is deliberate.

sections.title: SSD and NVMe
sections.body: Flash has no moving parts, so random access is fast; but it is erased in large blocks and wears out, so a controller spreads writes (wear levelling). NVMe attaches flash over PCIe with deep parallel queues, removing the SATA bottleneck. Cost per bit: HDD cheapest, SSD middle, RAM dearest.

questions.prompt: Why do elevator algorithms matter little on an SSD?

choices.text: There is no arm to move, so request order barely changes latency.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Seek time was the thing being optimised.
